passages.title: Three Hives on the Roof
passages.passage:
When my uncle Tuan told the family that he was going to keep bees on the roof of his apartment building, my grandmother laughed and said he would be stung to death in a week. That was two years ago. Today there are three wooden hives up there, and my grandmother puts his honey in her tea every morning.

Uncle Tuan did not start by buying bees. He spent a whole winter reading and watching videos, and then joined a small club of beekeepers who meet once a month in a park. An older member gave him his first colony in April, when the weather was warm and there were plenty of flowers on the trees along the streets. "Bees do not care whether they live in the countryside or in a city," the man told him. "They only care about food and a dry home."

The work is lighter than most people imagine. In spring and summer, my uncle opens each hive every ten days or so to check that the queen is laying eggs and that the bees have enough space. He wears a white suit with a net over his face, but he says the bees are usually calm if he moves slowly and does not open the hive on a cloudy day. In winter, he hardly touches the hives at all; the bees stay inside in a tight ball to keep warm, and he simply makes sure they have enough honey left to eat.

The first harvest was a surprise. From three hives he collected almost forty kilograms of honey, far more than one family could use. He gave jars to the neighbours, who had at first been nervous about living under thousands of insects. Now several of them have planted flowers on their balconies, and one young couple downstairs has asked him to teach them.

My uncle says the honey is only part of the reward. "The bees have made me notice things," he told me. "Which trees are flowering, when it is going to rain. I never looked at the city that way before."

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why honey from city bees tastes better than honey from the countryside
The dangers of keeping insects in a crowded apartment building
How a man started keeping bees in the city and what it brought him
A monthly beekeepers' club that meets in a public park
questions.explanation: Every paragraph follows Uncle Tuan's beekeeping: how he began, the work it involves, the harvest and what he learned. The club and the neighbours are details, and the passage never compares the taste of different honeys.

questions.q: How did Uncle Tuan get his first bees?
options: A young couple in his building offered them as a present.
He bought them after a winter of reading about them.
He caught a wild colony living in a tree in the park.
An experienced beekeeper from his club gave them to him.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says an older member of the club gave him his first colony in April. He read and watched videos first, but the passage says he did not start by buying bees.

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, why does Uncle Tuan avoid opening the hives on cloudy days?
options: The bees are more likely to be calm only in good weather.
The queen stops laying eggs when the sun is not out.
The honey becomes too thick to collect in cool weather.
He cannot see the eggs clearly without bright sunlight.
questions.explanation: He says the bees are usually calm if he moves slowly and does not open the hive on a cloudy day, so cloudy weather makes them less calm. Nothing is said about the queen, the honey or visibility.

questions.q: The word "harvest" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
options: visit
collection
winter
hive
questions.explanation: "The first harvest" is followed by "he collected almost forty kilograms of honey", so a harvest here is the collecting of the honey. It is not a place, a season or a visit.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the neighbours?
options: They refused to accept the jars of honey.
They have all started keeping bees on their own balconies.
Their feelings about the bees have changed since the first harvest.
They complained to the building manager about the hives.
questions.explanation: They were "at first nervous", but now several plant flowers for the bees and one couple wants lessons, which shows their attitude has changed. Only one couple asked to learn, not everyone, and no complaint is mentioned.

questions.q: Uncle Tuan checks the hives more often in winter than in summer.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says he opens the hives every ten days in spring and summer but "hardly touches" them in winter, so the statement is the opposite of what the passage says.

questions.q: Uncle Tuan sells his honey at the monthly club meeting.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says he gave jars to the neighbours, but it never mentions selling honey anywhere, so we cannot say whether this is true or false.

passages.title: The Village Above the Clouds
passages.passage:
Sin Ho is a village of about forty houses that sits on a shelf of land 1,500 metres above the valley floor. On most mornings, the villagers wake up above a sea of white cloud, and the fields below cannot be seen until the sun has been up for two or three hours. Visitors often say it looks like an island floating in the sky.

Life here follows the seasons more closely than it does in the towns. In spring, families plant rice on narrow terraces that were cut into the mountainside by their great-grandparents. In the hot months, the children lead water buffalo up to the high grass while the adults repair the stone walls that hold the terraces in place. The harvest in October is the busiest time of the year, and school closes for two weeks so that everyone can help.

Until 2015, the only way to reach Sin Ho was a footpath that took four hours to climb. Then a narrow road was built, and motorbikes could finally reach the village. The road changed many things. Fresh vegetables and medicine now arrive weekly, and the village has a small clinic with a nurse who comes every Tuesday. But the road also made it easier to leave. Several young people moved down to the town to find work, and two houses on the edge of the village now stand empty.

The village leader, Mrs Mai, believes the answer is tourism, but only a little of it. Last year, three families opened their homes to guests, who sleep on the wooden floor, eat with the family and are woken at dawn to watch the clouds. "We do not want a hotel," she says. "We want people to see how we live, and then go home."

So far, her plan seems to be working. One of the young men who left has returned to guide walkers, and the money from guests has paid for new roofs on four houses. The clouds, of course, cost nothing at all.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The building of a road to a village in 2015
Why young people are leaving Vietnam's mountain villages
The best time of year for tourists to see the clouds at Sin Ho
A mountain village, how it lives and how a new road has changed it
questions.explanation: The passage describes the village, its seasons, the effects of the road and the leader's plan. The road, the young people and tourism are each only part of that picture.

questions.q: Why does the school close for two weeks in October?
options: Because the road is blocked by cloud in the autumn
Because the children have to lead the buffalo to the high grass
Because everyone is needed for the rice harvest
Because the teacher leaves to work in the town
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the October harvest is the busiest time, and school closes "so that everyone can help". Leading the buffalo happens in the hot months, not October.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, the word "it" in "made it easier to leave" refers to
options: the village
leaving
the road
the clinic
questions.explanation: This "it" is an empty subject standing for the action "to leave": the road made leaving easier. The road is the thing that did the making, not what "it" refers to.

questions.q: What does Mrs Mai most likely mean by "only a little of it"?
options: She wants visitors, but not so many that the village changes.
She thinks tourism will bring in only a small amount of money.
She would prefer a small hotel rather than a large one.
She wants tourists to stay for only a short time each day.
questions.explanation: She says "We do not want a hotel. We want people to see how we live, and then go home," which shows she wants tourism kept small so village life stays the same. She rejects a hotel of any size.

questions.q: The word "terraces" in paragraph 2 refers to
options: wooden houses built on the edge of the village
paths that lead up to the high grass
walls made of stone to keep animals out
flat steps of land for growing crops on a slope
questions.explanation: Families "plant rice on narrow terraces that were cut into the mountainside", and stone walls hold them in place, so terraces are flat pieces of land for farming on the slope. The walls are separate from the terraces.

questions.q: Before 2015, it took about four hours on foot to reach Sin Ho.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 states that until 2015 the only way to the village was a footpath that took four hours to climb.

questions.q: The guests who stay in the village pay more than they would in a town hotel.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says money from guests paid for new roofs, but it never compares the price with a hotel, so there is no information to decide.

passages.title: The Bin Under the Sink
passages.passage:
For most of my life, our kitchen had one bin. Everything went into it: banana skins, plastic bottles, old newspapers and the foil from last night's dinner. Once a week my father carried the bag downstairs, and that was the end of the story. Then my younger sister came home from a school project and announced that our family was "doing it all wrong".

Her first idea was simple. She put three boxes under the sink and labelled them: paper, plastic and metal, and food. The food box went out every evening, because in our climate it starts to smell within a day. The other two were emptied only when they were full. Within a week we noticed something strange: the box for paper, plastic and metal filled up much faster than the one for food. We had never realised how much packaging we brought home from the supermarket.

Not everything went smoothly. My father kept dropping used tea bags into the plastic box, and I found out that greasy pizza boxes cannot be recycled with clean paper, no matter how carefully you fold them. My sister made a chart and stuck it on the fridge, with pictures for the things people got wrong most often. My grandmother, who cannot read English labels, found the pictures more useful than any of us.

The bigger change happened at the shops. Once you have to sort your rubbish, you start to see it before you buy it. My mother began choosing vegetables that were not wrapped in plastic, and we bought a large bottle of washing liquid instead of five small ones. Our weekly bag of real rubbish shrank to about half its old size.

My sister is now planning a compost box for the balcony, so that the food waste can feed her plants instead of going to the dump. My father says three boxes are enough for one apartment. I suspect she will win.

questions.q: What is the writer's main purpose in this passage?
options: To describe how one family began sorting its rubbish and what they learned
To persuade readers to build a compost box on their balcony
To complain about the amount of packaging supermarkets use
To explain the rules for recycling in the writer's city
questions.explanation: The writer tells the story of the family's change, from one bin to three boxes to shopping differently. Packaging and the compost box are parts of that story, not the aim of the whole passage.

questions.q: Why was the food box emptied every evening?
options: Because the family produced more food waste than anything else
Because food waste quickly begins to smell in a hot climate
Because the compost box on the balcony needed feeding
Because it was the smallest of the three boxes
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the food box went out every evening "because in our climate it starts to smell within a day". In fact the paper, plastic and metal box filled faster, and the compost box does not exist yet.

questions.q: Which of the following did the family discover could NOT be recycled?
options: Old newspapers
Used tea bags
Greasy pizza boxes
Foil from dinner
questions.explanation: The writer found out that greasy pizza boxes cannot be recycled with clean paper. Tea bags were put in the wrong box, but the passage does not say they cannot be recycled.

questions.q: Why did the grandmother find the chart especially useful?
options: She was the person who made the most mistakes.
She wanted to teach the rules to the writer's father.
She had never used a recycling box before.
She could understand the pictures even though she could not read the labels.
questions.explanation: The passage says she "cannot read English labels" and "found the pictures more useful than any of us", so the pictures helped her where words could not. The father, not the grandmother, is the one described making mistakes.

questions.q: The word "shrank" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
options: became smaller
disappeared
was thrown away
grew heavier
questions.explanation: The bag "shrank to about half its old size", so it became smaller. It did not disappear completely.

questions.q: The family now buys one large bottle of washing liquid instead of several small ones.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says they "bought a large bottle of washing liquid instead of five small ones".

questions.q: The writer's father has agreed to the plan for a compost box.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The father says three boxes are enough for one apartment, which means he is against the compost box. The writer only guesses that the sister will win.

passages.title: Fourteen Hours to the Coast
passages.passage:
The ticket said the journey would take twelve hours. It took fourteen, and I would not have wanted it to be any shorter.

I was travelling alone for the first time, going to stay with my cousin in a town on the coast. My mother had wanted me to fly, but the bus was a third of the price, and I had promised to pay for the trip myself. So at six in the evening I climbed into a sleeper bus with three rows of narrow beds and a driver who did not smile once.

For the first hour I stared at my phone. Then the signal disappeared as we entered the hills, and I had no choice but to look out of the window. The road twisted between dark shapes of mountains, and every so often we passed a village where a single light was still on. At a rest stop around midnight, an old woman in the bed next to mine shared her rice cakes with me and asked why I was travelling alone. When I told her, she laughed and said she had done the same thing at fifteen, forty years earlier, and had never once regretted it.

I did not sleep well. The beds are made for people shorter than me, and the bus stopped several times to pick up passengers who seemed to appear from nowhere on the dark road. Somewhere around four in the morning, the driver put on loud music, perhaps to keep himself awake. Nobody complained.

Then, just after sunrise, the mountains ended. The road dropped down towards a flat green plain, and in the far distance I saw a thin silver line that could only be the sea. The old woman was awake too. "Worth it?" she asked. I nodded.

My cousin was waiting at the station with a motorbike and a bottle of water. "You look terrible," he said. I told him I felt wonderful. Next time, I think, I will take the bus again.

questions.q: Which sentence best describes the passage?
options: A comparison of the cost of travelling by bus and by plane
The story of a teenager's first long journey alone and how it felt
A description of a friendship between a girl and an old woman
A warning about the dangers of night buses on mountain roads
questions.explanation: The writer describes the whole journey, from choosing the bus to arriving, and ends by saying they would do it again. The price and the old woman are parts of the story, not its subject.

questions.q: Why did the writer choose the bus instead of the plane?
options: The writer was paying and the bus was much cheaper.
There were no flights to the coastal town.
The writer wanted to meet other travellers.
The writer's mother preferred it.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the bus was a third of the price and the writer had promised to pay for the trip. The mother actually wanted the writer to fly.

questions.q: What made the writer stop looking at the phone?
options: The bus stopped at a rest stop.
The driver asked everyone to turn off their phones.
The old woman started a conversation.
The phone lost its signal in the hills.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the signal disappeared as they entered the hills, so the writer "had no choice but to look out of the window". The old woman spoke later, at the midnight stop.

questions.q: Why does the writer most likely mention that "Nobody complained" about the loud music?
options: To criticise the passengers for being too polite
To show that the passengers were all asleep
To suggest the passengers understood the driver needed to stay awake
To show that the music was not really very loud
questions.explanation: The writer guesses the music was "perhaps to keep himself awake", and the fact that nobody complained suggests the passengers accepted this. The writer was awake and describes the music as loud.

questions.q: The word "regretted" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
options: repeated
felt sorry about
been proud of
forgotten
questions.explanation: The old woman had "never once regretted" travelling alone at fifteen, meaning she was never sorry she did it. This fits her cheerful, encouraging attitude.

questions.q: In paragraph 5, what does "it" in "Worth it?" refer to?
options: The long, uncomfortable journey
The ticket price
The view of the sea
The rice cakes
questions.explanation: The old woman asks the question as the sea appears, meaning "was the difficult journey worth it?". The view is the reward, not the thing being paid for.

questions.q: The bus arrived at the coast two hours later than the ticket said.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The ticket said twelve hours and the journey took fourteen, which is two hours longer.
